abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The metabolome is highly diverse and the closest layer to phenotype; therefore, it is commonly regarded as a bridge between the genome and phenome in plants. Here, we performed large‐scale metabolome analysis using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and 33 grain‐related traits in a diverse panel of natural accessions and a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population. We identified a new network of 2286 associations between 947 metabolites and 33 grain‐related traits. Systematic integration of metabolic genome‐wide association study (mGWAS) and metabolic quantitative trait locus (mQTL) analyses identified 33 566 significant single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 3128 mQTL. Thirteen annotated metabolites co‐localized within a physical interval on 7A. Integration of metabolite‐based and phenotype‐based GWAS and QTL revealed an overlapped region for gibberellin A4 (GA4) content and grain roundness on 4A. Phenotyping of an ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)‐induced mutant confirmed the role of TaSDR in regulating GA4 content and grain morphology. These findings provide novel insights into the metabolic pathways influencing key grain‐related traits and advance our understanding of the complex molecular mechanisms regulating grain metabolites and phenotypes in wheat. The identified metabolic markers and candidate genes provide valuable targets for molecular breeding programs aimed at improving wheat yield and quality.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Wheat stands as a vital staple crop grown worldwide, providing approximately 20% of daily caloric intakes and 15% of protein in the human diet. Given the expanding population, change in diet preferences, and frequent episodes of weather extremes, breeding programs should align objectives for simultaneously improving yield, quality, and resilience (Rasheed et al. 2025). Grain morphological and quality traits are critical determinants of yield, and the genetic mechanisms underlying these traits have long been a major focus of research. Nevertheless, the acquisition of phenotypic data remains challenging due to the lack of standard protocols among labs and the inefficiency of existing methodologies (Song et al. 2021). Therefore, the development of biomarkers associated with agronomic traits may provide an effective solution.

The plant metabolome is widely recognized as the bridge between the genome and phenome because it directly reflects physiological and developmental changes during plant growth (Chen et al. 2014; Luo 2015; Razzaq et al. 2021; Sharma et al. 2021). Changes in metabolite composition reflect dynamic processes associated plant growth, development, and response to stress (Nadella et al. 2012). Moreover, metabolomics‐assisted breeding can be applied to crop species to predict complex agronomic traits (Matsuda et al. 2012; Shi et al. 2020; Yin et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2024) and accelerate crop improvement (Fernie and Schauer 2009). Therefore, integrating metabolomic, phenotypic, and genetic data can provide deeper insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying traits variations.

Recent advances in high‐throughput profiling and genotyping have facilitated the systematic analysis of the genetic basis of metabolite and agronomic trait variation. Previous studies have demonstrated the value of integrating metabolite, phenotype and genetic data in crops (Luo 2015; Yang et al. 2017; Yin et al. 2024; Shi, Hu, et al. 2025; Wang, Kang, et al. 2025). In wheat, quantitative trait loci (QTL) associated with both metabolites and agronomic traits have been identified (Hill et al. 2015, 2013). Shi et al. (2020) reported a candidate gene that may regulated tryptophan‐related metabolism and grains per spike. Studies in rice and maize have also shown that metabolite variation can be genetically linked to grain‐related traits and can provide informative biomarkers for breeding (Chen et al. 2016; Wen et al. 2014). More recently, integrated multi‐omics approaches have been employed to dissect the genetic basis of wheat grain and yield‐related traits, revealing novel metabolite‐trait associations and candidate genes that may facilitate the prediction of complex agronomic performance and accelerate crop improvement (Chen et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024; Wang, Li, et al. 2025). Collectively, these studies demonstrated that integrating metabolomics with other high‐throughput technologies can substantially enhances the toolkit available for genomics‐assisted selection (Fernie and Schauer 2009).

To date, the application of metabolomics in wheat research remains limited, particularly in revealing the relationship between grain metabolites and grain‐morphological traits. Existing studies have generally examined metabolic or agronomic traits independently, and relatively few have systematically integrated metabolic genome‐wide association study (mGWAS), phenotypic genome‐wide association study (pGWAS), metabolic quantitative trait locus (mQTL) and phenotypic quantitative trait locus (pQTL) analyses to identify shared loci and validate their effects in both association and linkage populations. Consequently, the metabolic basis of variation in wheat grain morphology as well as the genetic loci linking metabolite accumulation to grain‐related phenotypes remains unclear.

In the present study, we performed parallel mGWAS and pGWAS analyses of grain‐related traits in wheat and further validated co‐localized genomic intervals using mQTL and pQTL mapping. Our findings led to the identification and annotation of metabolites and candidate genes associated with key metabolic and phenotypic traits. These results provide valuable insights into the genetic architecture underlying metabolite variation and advance the prediction of grain‐related traits based on metabolite profiles.

sec.title: Variation in Grain‐Related Traits in Chinese Wheat
sec.p: We investigated a total of 33 traits, encompassing 12 grain morphology traits measured using a SeedCount SC600R image analyser (Figure S1A) and 21 flour quality traits in association panel (AP) consisting of 349 Chinese wheat accessions evaluated in at least two independent environments (Table S1). The flour quality traits included starch pasting properties, damaged starch content, and dough rheological properties (Figure S1B). Phenotype analysis revealed extensive natural variation for both trait categories (Figure S1C), with coefficients of variation (CVs) of 1.19%–191.58%, highlighting the broad phenotypic diversity within the panel (Table S2). For grain morphology, roundness varied from 0.59 to 0.86, with corresponding ranges of 5.89–7.32 mm for grain length, 2.98–3.72 mm for grain width, 2.75–3.45 mm for grain thickness, and 31.95–56.15 g for thousand‐grain weight. Flour quality traits also showed substantial variation, with setback viscosity (an indicator of starch retrogradation) ranging from 383.5 to 1847 centipoise (cP), damaged starch content ranging from 3.1% to 27.5%, and dough stability time ranging from 1.65 to 10.84 min. Correlation analysis indicated that most traits within the categories of grain morphology, starch pasting properties, and dough rheological properties were positively correlated with one another (Figure 1A). In contrast, significant negative correlations were observed between starch pasting properties and dough rheological properties. Collectively, this study reveals substantial phenotypic diversity and highlights a trade‐off between starch pasting properties and dough strength, providing insights for targeted wheat improvement.

sec.title: Metabolic Profile in Wheat Grain
sec.p: We performed a liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS)‐based widely targeted metabolomics assay (Shi et al. 2020) to profile metabolites in wheat grain of an association panel (AP) containing 349 accessions and a recombinant inbred line (XX‐RIL, Xiangyangdasui/Xinmai26) population comprising 138 lines, with three biological replicates. Totally, we identified 947 distinct metabolite features, of which 159 metabolites were structurally identified using authentic chemical standards and 302 were putatively annotated based on their mass spectral characteristics (Table S3). The structurally identified and putatively annotated metabolites (n = 461) were classified into 11 major biochemical categories (Figure 1B). Metabolite profiling revealed diverse metabolite composition, with the ‘Other’ category constituting the largest proportion (18%), followed by flavonoids (16%), amino acids and derivatives (11%), phytohormones and its derivatives (11%), lipids (10%), polyphenols (9%), nucleic acid derivatives (7%), phenolamides (7%), and vitamins (5%). Since metabolites in the ‘Other’ category could not be confidently assigned to the major chemical classes, their potential pathway associations were further annotated in Table S4.

Comparative analysis revealed distinct metabolite accumulation patterns between the AP and XX‐RIL populations (Figure 1C, Table S5). Metabolite variation was generally greater in the AP (CV range: 11.09%–618.76%) than in the XX‐RIL (CV range: 9.73%–569.28%). The greater metabolic diversity in the AP was possibly attributed to its broader genetic background. These findings demonstrate substantially metabolic diversity in wheat grains. Correlation analysis of the 461 annotated metabolites revealed that metabolites involved in sugar metabolism generally showed negative or weak correlations with those involved in other metabolic pathways. This pattern is consistent with competition for carbon precursors and energy between sugar metabolism and various biosynthetic processes (Figure 1D). In contrast, strong positive correlations (r > 0.9) were predominantly observed among metabolites within the same biochemical class (Figure 1D), indicating regulation and shared distribution patterns attributable to common biosynthetic origins or functional pathways. Notably, lipids constituted the largest proportion of these strongly correlated metabolite clusters (Figure 1E). Specifically, one prominent co‐regulatory network was centred on linoleic acid (mr1054) metabolism and glycerophospholipid remodelling, encompassing lysophospholipids such as lysoPE 16:0 (mr0437) and lysoPC 16:1 (mr0140). Beyond lipid‐lipid interactions, a distinct cross‐pathway correlation signature was identified (Figure 1F), highlighting tryptophan (mr1346) as a highly connected node. This aromatic amino acid showed strong correlations with its direct derivatives, such as 3‐indoleacetonitrile (mr650) and golotimod (mr1974), and further extended to downstream quinoline alkaloids, including 6‐methylquinoline (S19‐0999) and 6‐methoxyquinoline (R11‐0143).

sec.title: Relationship Between Metabolites and Grain‐Related Traits
sec.p: A large‐scale Pearson correlation analysis was performed to characterize the association between 947 metabolites and 33 grain‐related traits in the AP (Figure 2A, Table S6). The analysis revealed 2286 significant correlations, of which 110 metabolites were significantly correlated with more than two traits across multiple environments (Table S7). Notably, grain roundness was positively correlated with mr1054 (linoleic acid), mr2161 (4‐hydroxybenzaldehyde), and GA4 (gibberellin A4) (Figure 2B), and so forth. Grain length was negatively correlated with mr042 (flavonoid), mr1159 (polyphenol) and mr1049 (other pathways), and so forth. Grain width, grain thickness and thousand‐grain weight (Figure 2C) were all negatively correlated with mr042, mr1146, and mr232 (flavonoid pathway), mr4029 and mr4030 (phytohormone pathway), and so forth. Additionally, metabolites associated with both grain shape and quality traits were identified. For instance, mr048, mr1097, and mr1092 from the flavonoid pathway exhibited positive correlations with flour quality traits but negative correlations with grain traits. Conversely, GA4 was positively correlated with grain roundness, consistent with the known role of gibberellins in promoting cell elongation. Furthermore, we found that metabolites associated with the flavonoid pathway (mr1070, mr1149) and the phytohormone and its derivative (mr2098) pathway also showed negative correlations with grain width in both the AP and XX‐RIL populations (Tables S8 and S9).

sec.title: mGWAS and mQTL Analysis for Metabolome Profiling in Wheat Grains
sec.p: To elucidate the genetic variation underlying wheat grain metabolome composition, a metabolic genome‐wide association study (mGWAS) was performed in the AP using the wheat 660K SNP array. The analysis identified 33 566 SNPs associated with multiple metabolites. The subgenomes A (11,969) and B (12,362) harboured substantially more SNPs than the D subgenome (9234), indicating a subgenome bias. The phenotypic variation explained (PVE) by these SNPs reached 55.6%, with an average PVE of 20.4% (Table S10). Among the 11 major biochemical categories, metabolites classified as ‘Other’ contained the largest number of significant SNPs (9520), followed by amino acids derivatives (4719), flavonoids (4661) and nucleic acid derivatives (4349). Notably, 45.73% of the significant SNPs were associated with at least two metabolites (Table S11). Several loci, including AX‐111393788, AX‐110133791 and AX‐108763767 on 7D, AX‐109098888 on 3A, and AX‐110900527 on 3D, were associated with more than 100 annotated metabolites, suggesting their importance in regulating metabolic processes.

In the XX‐RIL population, joint linkage and association analysis identified 3128 QTL (Table S12) and 2011 significant SNPs (p < 0.001; Table S13) for 947 metabolites (Figure 3A). These QTL and SNPs were distributed across all 21 wheat chromosomes, with PVE values of 1%–55.67%. Notably, 207 QTL were detected in more than two metabolic pathways. However, several metabolites exhibited a single major QTL, including QTL for OxIAA on chromosome 4D (PVE = 50%) and mr1170 on chromosome 2B (PVE = 25%), suggesting that many QTL control more than one metabolite, possibly because of the high correlation among metabolites. Among the 11 major biochemical categories, metabolites classified as ‘Other’ contained the largest number of QTL (319), followed by flavonoid (246), lipids (179), and amino acids derivatives (171).

sec.p: Integrative analysis of the mGWAS results from the AP natural population and joint linkage and association analysis results from the XX‐RIL population identified 32 metabolites belonging to 10 categories (Figure 3B, Table S14). Further analysis revealed that these metabolites were co‐localized within several pleiotropic genomic regions (red rectangles in Figure 3A), where QTL for multiple metabolites were clustered. Integration of mGWAS and mQTL results showed that 167 metabolites were co‐localized within 89 genomic intervals. To further characterize the biological relevance of the co‐localized metabolite clusters, we examined the pathway annotations of metabolites within and across genomic regions. First, metabolites belonging to the same or similar pathways were frequently co‐localized within individual intervals (e.g., tryptophan and several indole‐related metabolites were co‐localized on 7A). Second, some chromosomal intervals contained distinct metabolites (e.g., the interval on 3D identified by AX‐110900527 was associated with lipid‐, flavonoid‐, and phenolic compound‐related metabolites). Third, metabolites from the same pathway, particularly flavonoid‐related metabolites, were identified at multiple independent genomic regions, including chromosomes 1B, 1D, 3D, 4D, 5B, and 6A. Collectively, these patterns suggest that the co‐localized intervals represent importantly genetic regulatory networks of metabolites.

To further explore the co‐localized region, 17 metabolites were mapped to genomic intervals of less than 5 Mb (Table S15). Of them, 13 metabolites from different pathways were significantly correlated with one another (r > 0.5, p < 0.001; Figure 3C). Integration of the results revealed that these 13 metabolites were consistently mapped to the same interval, spanning 27.19–30.28 Mb on chromosome 7A (Figure 3D,E) and covering 43 genes (IWGSCv 1.1). Within this interval, four distinct haplotype blocks were identified. Among them, only Block1 showed significant associations with nine of the 13 metabolites (Figures 3F and S2). Further dissection of Block1 revealed two haplotypes, with 7A_Hap1 identified as the superior allele (Figure 3G,H). Within Block1 (27.43–27.84 Mb), six candidate genes were identified (Table S16). Analysis of sequencing results by the wheat Pan800K Gene array showed that these six genes covered 1070 variants forming nonsynonymous or deleterious mutations in AP. After incorporating these 1070 variants to re‐run GWAS, TraesCS7A02G057300 (encoding a zinc finger GRF‐type domain‐containing protein, TaZGRF‐7A) was identified as the strongest candidate gene associated with 11 metabolites (IAM, mr677, mr1428, S19‐0689, S19‐0999, R11‐0143, mr650, mr1346, S16‐2152, R11‐0712 and mr2051), supporting the prioritization of TaZGRF‐7A as a candidate (Table S17). Haplotype analysis of TaZGRF‐7A revealed that wheat accessions carrying TaZGRF‐7A‐Hap1, which was present in 49 out of 120 accessions (40.8%), exhibited significantly lower metabolite accumulation for nine target compounds than accessions carrying the other haplotype (Figure 3I,J). These results suggested that TaZGRF‐7A might play an important role in regulating the level of these nine metabolites.

sec.title: Dissecting Complex Grain‐Related Traits by Integrated GWAS and QTL Analyses of Phenotypic and Metabolite Data
sec.p: To dissect the genetic basis of grain‐related traits in wheat, we used 33 grain‐related traits to perform a phenotypic genome‐wide association study (pGWAS) in the AP population using the Wheat 660K SNP array. Large‐scale pGWAS detected 22 014 significant SNPs (Figure 4A, Table S18). Of all significant SNPs, 84.24% and 12.73% were associated with grain morphological and flour quality traits, respectively, whereas 3.03% were associated with both trait categories. Linkage analysis of 11 grain‐related traits in the XX‐RIL population across environments identified 313 QTL (Figure 4C), with the PVE values ranging from 1% to 65.62% (Table S19).

sec.p: To genetically link metabolites with grain‐related traits, we integrated the results and identified 1792 SNPs that were significant in both mGWAS and pGWAS analyses (Table S20), as well as 96 QTL detected in both mQTL and pQTL analyses (Table S21). Co‐localization results of mGWAS and pGWAS showed that 395 SNPs were concurrently associated with multiple metabolites and grain‐related traits (n > 10) and thus were defined as pleiotropic SNPs. Likewise, the co‐localization of mQTL and pQTL identified 29 hotspot intervals concurrently detected by multiple metabolites and grain‐related traits (n > 10). These pleiotropic SNPs and hotspot intervals were unevenly distributed on chromosomes (Figure S3), and they are mainly on 7D, 2D, and 4A (Tables S22 and S23). For example, AX‐110133791 on 7D was significantly detected for 42 times across multiple metabolites and grain‐related traits, and the interval spanning AX‐108735064 to AX‐109951021 on 4D was significantly detected for 38 times, suggesting that these regions may harbour genomic hubs underlying coordinated regulation of metabolite accumulation and grain‐related traits.

Further analysis of these co‐mapped SNPs and QTL revealed that grain width, grain thickness, grain roundness and starch pasting properties were predominantly associated with metabolites in ‘Other’ pathway; thousand kernel weight was associated with metabolites in the nucleic acid derivative pathway; grain colour and seed area were closely associated with metabolites in the lipid pathway; and grain length was closely associated with metabolites in the flavonoid pathway (Figure 4B). Notably, the largest number of co‐mapped genetic loci was identified between dough rheological properties and metabolites in the phytohormone pathway and its derivatives.

To identify candidate genes that may simultaneously influence grain‐related traits and metabolite contents, we further analysed the physical locations of the co‐mapped SNPs and QTL. Further examination of trait‐specific associations (Table S22) revealed that SNPs associated with dough stability time co‐mapped with SNPs associated with metabolite n03958 in the 408.07–416.22 Mb region of chromosome 1D and with the polyphenol pathway metabolite S18‐2777 on 5A. SNPs associated with grain roundness co‐localized with SNPs associated with the phytohormone‐related compounds salicylic acid (SA) and gibberellin A4 (GA4) in the 20.99–21.19 Mb region of chromosome 1A and the 621.84–624.69 Mb region of chromosome 4A, respectively. Similarly, SNPs associated with grain length were also associated with the lipid metabolism‐related metabolite 2‐amino‐1,3,4‐octadecanetriol (S18‐0043) within a narrow interval on 2B (773.35–773.71 Mb). Among the co‐mapped QTL (Table S23), several regions were associated with more than four grain morphology traits and multiple metabolites. Notably, a QTL located on 4D within the 11.87–16.59 Mb interval was associated with six grain morphology traits and 20 metabolites from multiple metabolic pathways, all within a relatively narrow physical region of 4.72 Mb. Collectively, these findings reveal some genomic regions showing associations between metabolic pathways and agronomically important grain‐related traits, and provide promising targets for identifying candidate genes with pleiotropic effects or closely linked regulatory functions.

sec.title: Validation of Candidate Gene by Phenotyping of EMS‐Mutants
sec.p: Notably, the SNP and QTL results of Gibberellin A4 (GA4) and grain roundness were co‐mapped within the 621.8–624.7 Mb interval on chromosome 4A (Figure 4D, Table S24). Furthermore, this genomic interval contained a single haplotypes block comprising two haplotypes, with 4A_Hap2 showing higher GA4 content and grain roundness values (Figure 4E,F). This region harboured 33 genes (Table S25), of which 22 were expressed in wheat grain based on transcriptome data from the WheatOmics database (http://wheatomics.sdau.edu.cn). Sequencing using the wheat Pan800K Gene array showed that these 22 genes covered 2503 variants, including synonymous or deteriorated mutations in the AP. After adding these 2503 variants to re‐run GWAS, only TraesCS4A02G343700 (Short‐chain dehydrogenase/reductase family protein, TaSDR) was significantly associated with GA4 content and grain roundness. Haplotype analysis showed that eight variants in TaSDR formed three haplotypes (Figure 4G), and TaSDR‐Hap1 was associated with relatively higher GA4 content and grain roundness, indicating that TaSDR‐Hap1 is a superior haplotype. Its frequency in the AP was 32.9%.

We next screened the TaSDR mutant K3716 from the EMS‐mutagenized Kronos library (Figure 4H, Table S26). Compared with the wild type, K3716 showed reduced GA4 content (by 3.45%, p = 5.70 × 10−5) and decreased grain roundness (by 3.18%, p = 0.034) (Figure 4I–L), grain width (by 10.94%, p = 0.018), grain thickness (by 9.66%, p = 0.017) and thousand‐kernel weight (by 27.07%, p = 0.014), but did not show a significant change in grain length (Figure S4A,B). These findings indicate that TaSDR is associated with the maintenance of GA4 accumulation and thus positively regulates grain size.

To determine whether exogenous GA4 could rescue the loss of grain roundness of the TaSDR mutant, we applied exogenous GA4 to K3716 plants by foliar spraying. The GA4‐treated mutant showed significant increase in several agronomic traits, including grain roundness (Figure 4M), grain length, grain width, grain thickness (Figures 4N and S4C–E), and thousand kernel weight (Figure 4O). These results suggest that exogenous GA4 can partially rescue the reduced grain roundness of the TaSDR mutant. Taken together, our findings support that TaSDR is involved in GA4 accumulation and grain morphology.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Wheat grains synthesize a wide range of metabolites, and investigating metabolic variation across cultivars can provide valuable insights for improving grain quality and yield in breeding programs. However, most studies integrating metabolic and phenotypic traits with genomic approaches have been conducted using a single type of populations (Hill et al. 2015; Shi et al. 2020). To date, the combined use of metabolic and phenotypic data from both genome‐wide association study (GWAS) and QTL mapping to elucidate the genetic mechanisms underlying complex traits in wheat remains largely unexplored. In this study, we collected metabolomic and phenotypic data from natural population and a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population, combined these data with genotyping data generated using wheat 660 K single‐nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array. We then investigated correlations between metabolites and agronomic traits, as well as gene‐metabolite and gene‐metabolite‐agronomic trait associations. Our findings reveal novel genetic determinants and provide mechanistic insights into grain‐related and metabolic traits in wheat.

sec.title: Correlations Between Metabolic Traits and Grain Related Traits
sec.p: The plant metabolome serves as a readout of physiological status and functions as a bridge between the genome and the phenome. According, metabolites may act either as functional intermediates in biological pathways or as correlated biomarkers of phenotypic traits (Luo 2015). To date, considerable efforts have been devoted to characterizing the relationships between phenotypic and metabolic traits in plants. For instance, studies in potato have established associations between starch‐ and cold‐sweetening related traits and primary metabolites (Carreno‐Quintero et al. 2012, 2013). In rice, positive correlations were identified between C‐hexosyl‐chrysoeriol O‐hexoside and hull colour, as well as between trigonelline content and grain width (Chen et al. 2016). Similarly, research in wheat revealed significant correlations between grain number per spike and specific metabolites including 4‐indolecarbaldehyde (wm0034) and tryptophan (mr1346) (Shi et al. 2020). These findings establish novel metabolic‐phenotypic linkages and provide potential biomarkers for improving agronomic traits in wheat.

In this study, we identified a total of 2286 significant correlations between metabolic and phenotypic traits, with 110 metabolites showing associations with the same grain‐related traits across different environments. Notably, most of these metabolites were classified as flavonoids, phytohormones (including their derivatives), amino acid derivatives, lipids and others pathway. Further analysis revealed distinct patterns of phenotypic associations. Flavonoid‐ and phytohormone‐related metabolites exhibited broad negative associations with both grain morphology traits (roundness, thickness, and thousand‐kernel weight) and grain colour (CIE L, a, and b). Amino acid derivatives were significantly negatively associated with grain colour (CIE L and b); whereas metabolites involved in lipid pathways were mainly positively associated with flour quality traits (water absorption and dough stability time). Trade‐off between the biosynthesis of these metabolites and grain‐related traits have also been reported in previous studies. Matus‐Cádiz et al. (2008) demonstrated that accumulation of flavonols and proanthocyanidins leads to dark bran colour in white wheat, showing that phenolic compounds can negatively affect grain colour. In barley, Kelly et al. (2025) showed that strigolactone directly represses grain size during grain development. In wheat, protein content has been reported to be significantly negatively correlated with starch pasting properties (Liu et al. 2022) and grain colour (Sgaramella et al. 2023). Yazar and Kokini (2026) further demonstrated that endogenous wheat flour lipids play an important role in baked product quality, even though they constitute a minor fraction of wheat flour. Collectively, these findings suggest that plants have evolved intrinsic regulatory mechanisms to coordinate diverse metabolic pathways with grain‐related traits.

Rather than simply accumulating or reducing specific metabolites, plants finely tune the synthesis and allocation of flavonoids, phytohormones, proteins, and lipids according to their intrinsic regulatory logic, ultimately achieving an balance between growth, defence, and grain quality. By revealing metabolites that consistently show strong associations with key traits, these regulatory patterns may support the development of robust, high‐throughput biomarkers for rapid breeding selection without compromising yield potential. Therefore, the identification and validation of such biomarkers will be crucial for designing breeding strategies aimed at harmoniously improving multiple traits.

sec.title: Integrated Metabolite Genome‐Wide Association Study and Metabolite Quantitative Trait Locus Analysis
sec.p: The integrated application of metabolite genomic approaches, including genome‐wide association studies (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) analysis, has been extensively used to elucidate the genetic architecture of metabolic traits in model and crop species, including Arabidopsis (Lisec et al. 2007), sesame (Song et al. 2022), rice (Chen et al. 2014), maize (Chen et al. 2020; Wen et al. 2014), and wheat (Shi et al. 2020). These approaches have proven highly effective for characterizing metabolite diversity and elucidating the associations of metabolites with biotic‐ and abiotic‐stress responses (Chen et al. 2018; Glauser et al. 2011; Peng et al. 2017), food quality, and flavour (Peng et al. 2016; Sharma et al. 2016; Tieman et al. 2017). In wheat, most previous studies were conducted using recombinant inbred line (RIL) populations with a limited number of markers. Metabolite genome‐wide association studies (mGWAS) have previously been conducted in leaf tissues from 135 winter wheat accessions using 17 372 single‐nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers (Matros et al. 2017), and in grian tissues from 182 accessions using 14.646 SNP markers (Chen et al. 2020). Shi et al. (2020) and Hill et al. (2015) conducted metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) analysis using 119 001 SNP and 551 polymorphic markers, respectively, in 145 and 179 wheat lines. Our joint analysis provided new mechanistic insight into the genetic basis of the wheat grain metabolome and enabled cross‐validation of the identified loci. The resulting gene‐metabolome framework, comprising 33 565 significant SNPs and 3128 mQTL will facilitate future studies.

The integrated mGWAS and mQTL analyses further revealed that 167 annotated metabolites co‐localized within 89 genomic intervals, 17 of which were mapped to narrow regions (< 5 Mb). Among the metabolites located within these narrow intervals, 13 metabolites from different metabolic pathways were significantly correlated with one another (r > 0.5, p < 0.001). Based on their annotations, these 13 metabolites were mainly associated with tryptophan‐derived indole metabolism, nitrogen‐containing heterocycle metabolism, and phenylpropanoid‐related processes. Their accumulation may reflect shared regulation of aromatic amino acid metabolism, secondary metabolism, and stress‐responsive pathways. However, these correlations do not necessarily indicate direct biochemical conversions among the metabolites. Further investigation of the genomic intervals co‐mapped by the 13 metabolites identified TraesCS7A02G057300, which encodes a zinc finger protein containing a growth‐regulating factor (GRF)‐type domain, as a potential candidate gene underlying their accumulation.

GRF proteins are plant‐specific transcription factors characterized by two highly conserved domains: the WRC (Trp‐Arg‐Cys) domain, which is involved in DNA binding, and the QLQ (Gln‐Leu‐Gln) domain, which mediates protein–protein interactions and may facilitate the recruitment of SWI/SNF chromatin‐remodelling complexes to regulate transcription (Yan et al. 2021). In addition to their well‐established roles in regulating leaf growth, GRFs are also implicated in reproductive development, senescence, and developmental plasticity in response to environmental cues (Rodriguez et al. 2016). Given its putative role as a transcriptional regulator, we hypothesize that TraesCS7A02G057300 influences the accumulation of the associated metabolites by directly or indirectly modulating the expression of multiple biosynthetic or catabolic genes in the corresponding metabolic pathways.

We further integrated our mGWAS and mQTL results with the published mQTL data from Shi et al. (2020). This meta‐analysis revealed that the genetic loci for eight metabolites co‐localized within the same genomic interval (Table S27), indicating that the candidate genes underlying the variation in these metabolites are likely located in this region. The joint mGWAS and mQTL analysis provided valuable insights into the molecular basis of metabolic variation and the genetic architecture of key metabolic pathways in common wheat.

sec.title: Comparative Analysis of Metabolite and Phenotypic Genome‐Wide Association Studies and Quantitative Trait Locus Analyses
sec.p: Comparative analyses of metabolite genome‐wide association studies (mGWAS) and phenotypic genome‐wide association studies (pGWAS) can provide evidence of the genetic co‐regulation of metabolic and phenotypic traits (Schauer et al. 2006; Riedelsheimer et al. 2012; Chen et al. 2016; Shi et al. 2020). Most previous studies integrating mGWAS and pGWAS have been conducted in rice (Chen et al. 2016), maize (Wen et al. 2014), and tomato (Toubiana et al. 2012). Until now, only Shi et al. (2020) have reported the co‐localization of wm0034 (4‐indolecarbaldehyde), mr1346 (tryptophan), and grain number per spike within a 27.6‐Mb region on chromosome 4B in wheat. In this study, 33 grain‐related traits, encompassing grain morphology and flour quality parameters, were analysed together with 947 metabolic traits. Co‐localization analysis based on mGWAS and pGWAS identified 1793 significant single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 16 genomic intervals. Further investigation of these co‐mapped SNPs revealed systematic associations between metabolic pathways and grain‐related traits. For example, metabolites in the lipid pathway exhibited the strongest co‐localization with grain colour and seed area, whereas metabolites in the flavonoid pathway showed the strong association with grain length. Notably, dough rheological properties shared the largest number of co‐localized loci with metabolites in the phytohormone pathway and its derivatives. These findings demonstrate potential links between specific metabolic pathways and key agronomic traits.

Integrated analysis of mGWAS, pGWAS, metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) analyses, and phenotypic quantitative trait locus (pQTL) analyses further revealed that GA4 (gibberellin A4) and grain roundness co‐localized within the 621.8–624.7 Mb region on chromosome 4A. Gibberellic acids (GAs) are important plant hormones that function as endogenous regulators of plant growth and development (Singh et al. 2002). As a key member of this hormones class, GA4 can acts as a critical modulator of growth and physiological responses (Nani et al. 2022). Based on the identified interval, we took TraesCS4A02G343700 (TaSDR) as a promising candidate gene associated with both GA4 content and grain roundness. This gene encodes a member of the short‐chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family, which is involved in steroid biosynthesis. The encoded protein plays an important role in the brassinosteroid signalling pathway, where it contributes to the regulation of nuclear gene expression and modulates various aspects of plant growth and development (Tang et al. 2008).

To functionally validate this candidate, we analysed the ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)‐induced mutant K3716 of durum wheat cultivar Kornos, which carries a missense variant in TaSDR. Compared with the wild‐type, the mutant exhibited significantly reduced grain roundness, lower GA4 content, and a 27.07% reduction in thousand kernel weight. Besides, exogenous GA4 treatment altered grain roundness in the K3716 mutant. These findings suggest that TaSDR positively regulates GA4 accumulation, which in turn influences grain morphology, supporting the role of TaSDR as a regulator in the GA4‐mediated modulation of grain development. Nevertheless, the molecular basis underlying the regulation of GA4 accumulation and grain roundness by TaSDR remains to be fully elucidated and will require further functional studies.

sec.title: Potential Mechanisms Linking TaSDR to GA4 Metabolism
sec.p: The EMS mutant and exogenous GA4 treatment experiments provided evidence that TaSDR influences grain morphology and is associated with GA4 accumulation. To date, GA homeostasis has been shown to involve GA20‐oxidases (GA20ox) and GA3‐oxidases (GA3ox) in the biosynthesis of bioactive GAs, GA2‐oxidases (GA2ox) in GA deactivation, and the GID1 receptor, DELLA repressors, and SCF (SLY1/GID2) ubiquitin ligase complexes in GA signal transduction (Davière and Achard 2013; Hedden and Phillips 2000; Ueguchi‐Tanaka et al. 2005; Yamaguchi 2008). However, plant short‐chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) proteins have not yet been established as canonical components of GA biosynthesis, deactivation, or signalling pathways. The SDR superfamily comprises diverse NAD(P)‐dependent oxidoreductases involved in the metabolism of lipids, amino acids, carbohydrates, and phytohormones (Moummou et al. 2012). For example, the Arabidopsis gene ABA2 (also known as GIN1 or AtSDR1) encodes an SDR that catalyses the conversion of xanthoxin to abscisic aldehyde, a key step in ABA biosynthesis (Cheng et al. 2002). Its rice ortholog, OsABA2 (also referred to as OsSDR), performs the same enzymatic reaction, as supported by in vitro enzyme assays and complementation of the Arabidopsis aba2 mutant (Endo et al. 2014). These findings demonstrate that plant SDR proteins can function in phytohormone metabolism.

GA and ABA often exert antagonistic effects during plant growth and development, particularly in seed development, germination, and growth regulation. Alterations in ABA metabolism or ABA signalling may affect GA biosynthesis, GA deactivation, and GA responsiveness, whereas GA signalling can also modulate ABA‐associated developmental processes (Finkelstein and Rock 2002; Seo and Koshiba 2002; Sun 2008). Therefore, the association between TaSDR and altered GA4 accumulation may potentially result from changes in ABA homeostasis or ABA‐responsive regulatory pathways. Nevertheless, this hypothesis remains speculative because ABA contents and ABA‐related molecular responses were not examined in the present study. Future investigations integrating GA and ABA quantification, expression analyses of GA‐ and ABA‐related genes, and biochemical characterization of TaSDR will be necessary to determine whether TaSDR influences GA4 accumulation through direct effects on GA metabolism, ABA‐GA crosstalk, or modulation of GA signalling.

sec.title: Germplasm and Field Trials
sec.p: The association panel (AP) consisted of 349 representative wheat accessions, including 106 historical and 243 modern varieties from the Huanghuai Valley as we previously described (Shi, Li, et al. 2025; Zheng et al. 2026; Yang et al. 2025). Field trials were conducted at the Scientific Research and Education Center (SREC) of Henan Agricultural University in Xingxiang (35.15° N, 113.80° E), Jiaozuo (35.19° N, 113.21° E), and Shunyi (40.23° N, 116.56° E) during the 2015–2016 growing season; in Zhengzhou (34.76° N, 113.65° E) from 2017 to 2020; and in Luohe (33.58° N, 114.02° E) and Zhumadian (32.98° N, 114.02° E, including Xiping and Suiping) from 2017 to 2018, as well as in Yuanyang (35.11° N, 114.15° E) from 2018 to 2020. All trials followed a replicated design with two replications per location within each cropping season.

A recombinant inbred line (RIL) population consisting of 138 lines derived from the cross between Xiangyangdasui and Xinmai 26 (XX‐RIL) was used for metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) and phenotypic quantitative trait locus (pQTL) analyses. The RIL population was grown at the SREC of Henan Agricultural University in Yuanyang (35.11° N, 114.15° E) during the 2018–2020, 2021–2022, and 2023–2024 cropping seasons, with two replicates per line.

The wheat lines were arranged in a completely randomized block design. Each accession was planted in two rows, with 10 cm between plants in a row and 25 cm between adjacent rows. All the tested materials grew well under local management conditions. The accessions were harvested by hand when they reached full maturity in early June and subsequently threshed manually.

sec.title: Grain Morphology Analysis
sec.p: Grain morphology traits were determined using a SeedCount SC600R image analyser (Next Instruments, Australia) as we described previously (Niaz et al. 2023). This digital imaging system was developed specifically for the grain industry and can accurately analyse wheat grain morphological characteristics, including grain roundness, aspect ratio, length, width, thickness, thousand kernel weight, average seed area, total seed area, lightness (CIE L), redness (CIE a), and yellowness (CIE b). Grain roundness was calculated as (width/length + thickness/length + thickness/width)/3, and the aspect ratio was calculated as length/width. More than 20 g of cleaned grain were used for each accession.

sec.title: Flour Preparation
sec.p: The flour preparation procedure has been described in detail previously (Lv et al. 2021). For each accession, the hardness index (HI) was determined for 100 randomly selected seeds using a Single Kernel Characterization System 4100 (SKCS 4100, Perten Instruments, PerkinElmer). Kernel moisture content was measured by near‐infrared spectroscopy using a DA7200 instrument (Perten Instruments) and adjusted to standard levels of 12% for kernels and 14% for flour when flour quality was assessed. Wheat flour was produced from each sample using a CD1 Mill (Chopin Technologies, Paris, France) according to the procedure reported previously (Chen, Gong, et al. 2013; Lv et al. 2021).

sec.title: Determination of Pasting Properties
sec.p: A Rapid Visco Analyser‐TecMaster (RVA‐TecMaster, Perten Instruments) was used to examine the functional properties of starch (Balet et al. 2019). Approximately 3.5 g of flour from each sample was added to 25 mL of distilled water to prepare a 6% suspension on a dry weight basis (w/w). Each suspension was held at 50°C for 1 min, heated up to 95°C at a rate of 12°C/min, held at 95°C for 2.5 min and then cooled to 50°C at a rate of 12°C/min. Seven parameters were obtained from the pasting profile. These include peak temperature (PTe), defined as the temperature at which viscosity began to develop during heating; peak viscosity (PV) defined as the highest viscosity reached before cooling; peak time (PTi), defined as the time required to reach peak viscosity; final viscosity (FV), defined as the maximum viscosity reached after cooling; and trough viscosity (TV), defined as the minimum viscosity between PV and FV. Breakdown (BD) was calculated as PV‐TV, and setback (SB) was calculated as FV‐TV. Lower BD and SB values indicate greater paste stability and greater resistantance to retrogradation.

sec.title: Damaged Starch Content Analysis
sec.p: Damage starch content in wheat flour was analysed using an SDmatic instrument (Chopin Technologies) according to AACC Method 76‐30.02 (American Association of Cereal Chemists; http://methods.aaccnet.org/summaries/76‐30‐02.aspx). This method quantifies the percentage of starch granules susceptible to hydrolysis by fungal α‐amylase. For each sample, 3 g of boric acid (H3BO3), 3 g of potassium iodide (KI), one drop of 0.1 mol/L sodium thiosulfate (Na2O3S2) and 120 mL of double‐distilled water were mixed. All reagents were obtained from DAMAO Chemical Reagent Factory (Tianjin, China). Subsequently, 1 g of flour was added to the mixture. The SDmatic instrument automatically generated the following parameters: damaged starch content, expressed in Unité Chopin Dubois (UCD); corrected damaged starch content adjusted for flour moisture and protein, expressed in Unité Chopin Dubois correction (UCDc); and the percentage of iodine absorbed by damaged starch (absorbed iodine, AI%).

sec.title: Analysis of the Rheological Behaviour and Pasting Properties of Dough
sec.p: A Mixolab analyser (Chopin Technologies, France) was used to analyse the mixing properties of dough according to the Chopin+ protocol and AACC Method 54‐60.01. The protocol comprised five sequential phases: (1) initial mixing for 8 min at 30°C to evaluate dough formation and weakening (C1); (2) heating from 30°C to 60°C to evaluate gluten weakening as a function of torque reduction (C2); (3) gelatinization during heating from 60°C to 90°C to characterize starch gelatinization behaviour (C3); (4) holding at 90°C for 7 min to measure stability during heating (C4, stability time); (5) cooling to 50°C to assess starch retrogradation (C5). Torque was measured throughout the 45‐min mixing cycle. Water absorption (g/kg; weight of water in grams per kilogram of flour), stability time (min), C1 (N m), C2 (N m), C3 (N m), C4 (N m), and C5 (N m) were obtained directly from the instrument. The differences C2 − C1 (N m), C3 − C2 (N m), C4 − C3 (N m), and C5 − C4 (N m) were calculated. These parameters indicate protein‐network strength under increasing temperature and amylase activity associated with falling numbers (Švec and Hrušková 2015).

sec.title: Metabolites Determination Using LC–MS/MS
sec.p: Mature grains from 349 wheat accessions and 138 XX‐RIL lines were harvested for metabolomic analysis, with three biological replicates for each sample. After collection, mature grains were ground using a TissueLyser II homogenizer (Qiagen, Germany) at 29 Hz for 60 s. For metabolite extraction, 100 mg of grain powder was suspended in 1.0 mL of 70% methanol containing 0.1 mg/L acyclovir. The mixtures were vortexed and kept at 4°C overnight for extraction. After centrifugation at 9500× g for 10 min, the extracts were clarified by filtration through 0.22‐μm organic filters (SCAA‐104; ANPEL, China). The extracts were analysed by liquid chromatography–electrospray ionization–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–ESI–MS/MS) using a Shim‐pack UFLC–CBM20A high‐performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Shimadzu, Japan) coupled with a 5500 QTRAP mass spectrometer (Applied Biosystems, USA). The tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) library was established using stepwise multiple ion monitoring combined with enhanced product‐ion scanning, as described previously by Chen, Zhang, et al. (2013). Accurate precursor‐ion masses were additionally acquired using a TripleTOF 5600 platform to support metabolite identification. Metabolite levels were determined by scheduled multiple‐reaction monitoring (MRM) analysis using Analyst 1.5 software. The MRM detection window and target scan time were set to 90 s and 1.0 s, respectively. Metabolites were annotated by comparing their mass‐to‐charge ratios, fragmentation patterns, and retention times with those of authentic standards and entries in public databases, including METLIN, the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), and MassBank. Metabolites that could not be confidently assigned to these major classes were provisionally grouped as ‘Other’ and further putatively subclassified into biologically meaningful pathway groups using HMDB, KEGG, and PubChem databases. Metabolites for which no reliable pathway annotation could be assigned were retained as ‘NA’ to avoid overinterpretation. The detailed classification is provided in Table S4.

sec.title: Genotyping and Quality Control
sec.p: The association panel was genotyped using the Affymetrix Wheat 660K SNP array as we described previously (Sun et al. 2025, 2020; Zhao, Zheng, et al. 2023). High‐quality genomic DNA was extracted from young leaves of each line using the cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) method. Genotyping data quality control (QC) was performed using PLINK v1.9 software (Purcell et al. 2007). SNPs were filtered to exclude markers with a minor allele frequency (MAF) < 0.05 or a missing genotype rate > 10%. After filtering, 425 983 high‐quality SNPs were retained for downstream analyses. No individual was removed because of a high missing genotype rate (MIND > 0.1).

sec.title: Population Structure and Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) Analysis
sec.p: To evaluate population structure (Q), a subset of unlinked SNP markers was selected based on linkage equilibrium (r 2 = 0). Population structure was assessed using STRUCTURE version 2.3.4 (Pritchard et al. 2000). Ten independent replicates were performed for each assumed number of subpopulations (K = 1–10), with a burn‐in period of 10 000 iterations followed by 1000 Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) replicates. Linkage disequilibrium (LD) was estimated using PLINK v1.9 by calculating the squared correlation coefficient (r 2) between pairs of SNP loci across the A, B, and D genomes, following the method described by Weir (1996). The window size for LD calculation was determined based on the number of SNPs located on each chromosome. A sliding‐window approach was used to calculate pairwise r 2 values for all SNP pairs within each window. Genome‐wide LD decay distance was defined as the physical distance (in Mb) at which the average r 2 declined to half of its maximum value (Marone et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2014). Co‐localization was defined based on overlap between significant mGWAS signals and reported mQTL intervals. Specifically, a co‐localized region was defined as the physical overlap between an mGWAS‐associated interval, delineated by a cluster of consecutive significant SNPs, and a reported mQTL interval on the same chromosome.

sec.title: Genome‐Wide Association Study
sec.p: Genome‐wide association studies (GWASs) were performed using the GAPIT toolkit implemented in the R programming environment as we previously described (Zhao, Wang, et al. 2023). A mixed linear model (MLM) approach (Lipka et al. 2012) incorporating principal component analysis (PCA) and a kinship matrix (PCA + K) was used to account for population stratification and relatedness. Specifically, the first four principal components derived from the filtered SNP dataset comprising 425 983 SNPs were included as fixed‐effect covariates, whereas a genomic relationship matrix (K) estimated using the VanRaden method (VanRaden 2008) was included as a random‐effect term. This PCA + K approach has been widely adopted in crop GWAS to reduce false‐positive associations arising from population stratification. The p‐value threshold was determined using a modified Bonferroni correction implemented in the Genetic Type 1 Error Calculator, version 0.2, and was set at 1.0 × 10−4 to identify significant associations across biological replicates.

sec.title: Quantitative Trait Locus Analysis
sec.p: The XX‐RIL population was genotyped using the wheat 55 K SNP array, and 1739 SNPs were retained for construction of a high‐density genetic map (Zhao, Wang, et al. 2023). Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping was performed using inclusive composite interval mapping of the additive genetic model (ICIM‐ADD), implemented in ICIMapping version 4.0 (Li et al. 2007). The chromosome‐walking step for the genome‐wide scan was set to 1.0 centimorgan (cM), and the probability for stepwise regression (PIN) was set to 0.01 to control the entry of cofactors. A logarithm‐of‐odds (LOD) threshold of 2.5 was used to clarify significant QTLs controlling metabolite and grain‐related traits across environments.

sec.title: Validation of Candidate Genes Using Ethyl Methane Sulfonate Mutants
sec.p: A mutant of TraesCS4A02G343700 was screened from the ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)‐mutagenized tetraploid wheat Kronos mutation library (Henry et al. 2014). Mutants line K3716, which carried a missense variant (G235A), was selected for functional verification. The mutant was backcrossed twice with the wild‐type to remove background mutations, and the mutation site was confirmed by sequencing (Table S18). Ten days after pollination, a 0.007 g/L gibberellin A4 (GA4) solution was sprayed on K3716 and wild‐type plants. A second application was performed 10 days later. After grain maturation, the plants were threshed manually, and grain size was measured. GA4 (product code: GC15310‐1g) was purchased from Shanghai Guchen Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Metabolite data were log2‐transformed for further statistical analysis. Person correlation was performed in R to evaluate the relationships between grain quality traits and metabolites levels. Grain‐related traits associated with metabolites were identified using the criteria |r| > 0.3 and p < 0.05. Coefficients of variation were calculated using Excel and R. A correlation network among metabolites was constructed using Cytoscape. Heatmaps were generated using the online data analysis and visualization platform at https://www.bioinformatics.com.cn.

caption.p: Figure S1: Summary of the phenotypic parameters evaluated in the association panel and the XX‐RIL population. (A) Twelve grain morphology traits quantified using the SeedCount SC600R image analyser. (B) Twenty‐one indirect grain‐related traits, including starch pasting properties, damaged starch content, and dough rheological properties, measured using a Rapid Visco Analyser (RVA‐TecMaster), an SDmatic damaged starch analyser, and a Chopin Mixolab, respectively. (C) Phenotypic distributions of 33 grain‐related traits presented as raincloud plots. Each raincloud plot consists of a half‐violin plot displaying the probability density (‘cloud’), a box plot showing the median and interquartile range (‘box’), and jittered points representing individual observations (‘raindrops’).

Figure S2: Haplotype analysis of the four LD blocks within the 27.19–30.28 Mb interval on chromosome 7A. (A, B) Schematic representation of the four haplotype blocks (Blocks 1–4) identified within the 27.19–30.28 Mb genomic region on chromosome 7A, with physical positions indicated in Mb. (C–E) Association of haplotypes with the 13 correlated metabolites. Different lowercase letters indicate significant differences between haplotypes (p < 0.05, Student's t‐test). Data are presented as mean ± SD.
